findings.headline: {diy:uses} of {n_base} comments use or recommend a general AI tool for incident work ({diy:uses:positive} positive, {diy:uses:sceptical} sceptical), but only {diy:objection} raise "I could do this myself" as an objection.
findings.short: {diy:uses} of {n_base} engineers' comments use or recommend a general AI tool for incident work, yet only {diy:objection} call that a reason not to buy a dedicated product.
findings.implication: For these engineers the baseline is a general AI tool they already use, so the story has to show what Investigations adds over pasting an alert into one. incident.io already makes the argument: in-house tools rarely get their accuracy measured, and the value is in the work around the model. The next step is evidence, such as a side-by-side of a bare model and Investigations on the same past incidents, using the daily backtesting it describes.
findings.note: Phase 5 hostile review (20 Oct), shorter headline; implication reframed constructively (was 'these rest on unnamed anecdotes'). Hero line approved by Dany.

findings.headline: Since 2025, the second most common objection is that these tools deskill or replace engineers: {count_since_2025:deskills_or_replaces_engineers} of {base_since_2025} comments, close behind "AI can't do this job yet" ({count_since_2025:not_capable_yet}).
findings.implication: The fear is concrete: who debugs when the tool is wrong, or when the person on call never built the knowledge? incident.io says engineers keep the final call and that Nexus raises the floor for new hires, and one real-incident write-up shows a responder new to that code checking the conclusion before acting. Evidence that responders can explain the cause afterwards would answer the concern.
findings.note: Phase 5 hostile review (20 Oct), one quote was about AI-written code (now hidden); the implication misdescribed a real incident as a demo and mixed an all-time count into a since-2025 finding.

findings.headline: {either:wrong_or_hallucinated_cause+cant_verify_reasoning} of {n_base} comments say the AI gets the cause wrong or that its reasoning can't be checked; {sceptical:wrong_or_hallucinated_cause} of the {count:wrong_or_hallucinated_cause} about wrong causes are sceptical.
findings.implication: Engineers want more than fewer wrong answers: they want to see what was checked and ruled out. incident.io's pages say it had to engineer against hallucination, that every hypothesis links to its sources and shows the theories it ruled out, and that invented citations are now rejected. Publishing misses alongside hits, with the timeline of a call it got wrong, would persuade this audience more than success stories alone.
findings.note: Phase 5 hostile review (20 Oct), tighter wording; uses the site's own label words.
